tiles.heading: Look here first
tiles.details:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1259) — Follow the runners across the soil and check for underground stems too. The Flora describes both aboveground stolons and underground rhizomes.

First find slender aboveground stolons forming a dense mat, then a REAL connected root-emitting node and a pale scaly underground rhizome if available. At the blade/sheath junction find a tiny HAIR-FRINGED MEMBRANOUS rim (about 0.2–0.5 mm) with conspicuous longer collar hairs; the old photo shows the longer hairs, NOT a measured ligule. At bloom look for commonly 4–6 slender terminal ONE-SIDED fingers emerging nearly together. Other fingerhead grasses overlap: check Digitaria's staggered racemes, Eleusine's flattened whitish base, Chloris's separate whorls, and native buffalograss's separate male/female heads. An introduced bermudagrass turf cultivar or hybrid isn't always safely determinable from leaves or sterile lawn photographs.

tiles.heading: Flowering and seed structures
tiles.details:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1259) — Trace the flowering fingers to the tip of one stem. On a single flattened branch, look for two overlapping rows of spikelets, each with one awnless floret.

Terminal digitate or subdigitate panicle with usually 4–6 thin branches (extremes 2–9), mostly radiating from nearly one point; branches 2–6 cm, narrow and one-sided.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: 1. Recognize a short dense spreading turf patch (panel 1), but never ID a grass from mown turf color or density alone.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Terminal digitate or subdigitate panicle with usually 4–6 thin branches (extremes 2–9), mostly radiating from nearly one point; branches 2–6 cm, narrow and one-sided.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

panels.caption: An aboveground slender horizontal stem with attached narrow leaf blades is visibly held over fingers. This is a stolon/runner candidate; roots visibly growing from an attached node are NOT established here, and no underground rhizome is exposed.

intro: First find slender aboveground stolons forming a dense mat, then a REAL connected root-emitting node and a pale scaly underground rhizome if available. At the blade/sheath junction find a tiny HAIR-FRINGED MEMBRANOUS rim (about 0.2–0.5 mm) with conspicuous longer collar hairs; the old photo shows the longer hairs, NOT a measured ligule. At bloom look for commonly 4–6 slender terminal ONE-SIDED fingers emerging nearly together. Other fingerhead grasses overlap: check Digitaria's staggered racemes, Eleusine's flattened whitish base, Chloris's separate whorls, and native buffalograss's separate male/female heads. An introduced bermudagrass turf cultivar or hybrid isn't always safely determinable from leaves or sterile lawn photographs.
memory_rule: BERMUDA CANDIDATE = fine turf mat + surface stolon + short fringed ligule/collar hairs + 4–6 fine ONE-SIDED flowering fingers from about one point. Expose a TRUE scaly underground rhizome and a truly root-emitting surface node before claiming full runner anatomy.
safety_note: Existing six images prove selected gross features and hair tufts, not the same plant's true attached roots/rhizome; lawn species/hybrid identity remains source-provisional. The tiny C. dactylon ligule is often described as a ciliolate membrane ~0.2–0.5 mm; do not assert absolutely NO membrane. Finger heads, runner or collar hair alone are not conclusive, and buffalograss can also have short hairy ligules.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
